doc.title: Butch Miles interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Drummer influences: Krupa, Morello, Bellson, Rich and others
summary: He names Gene Krupa as his first big influence and lists other drummers, working backwards in time to the 1920s and 30s.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Who were some of the influential drummers that you listened to that you liked at that time?

Well my first big influence was Gene Krupa. He was like the biggest influence on me. Right at the beginning I was a huge fan of Gene’s. I loved everything about him. I loved his style and his sound, and his flair, his showmanship, and the way he would really put over a great drum solo — even add that little extra pizzazz that just made me say “Wow.” Because a lot of times you see some wonderful musicians and they just look like they can’t wait for the next taxi out of town. They’re not enjoying themselves or having any good time or communicating a lot that way with an audience. They let the music do all the talking. That’s absolutely fine, that’s wonderful, but I like to see a little show business thrown in there too. And then I was very big fan of Joe Morello’s and Louie Bellson, and a little bit later, Buddy Rich, once I began to understand what he was doing. What he was playing was way above my head. I couldn’t understand it. And then I got into Roy Haynes, I loved Papa Jo Jones, Philly Joe Jones, Baby Dodds, Chick Webb, you know the list is pretty endless. There’s almost no drummer that I don’t admire, living or dead.
From that list it’s almost as if you went backwards in first listening to like Krupa and then listening to guys that came even before him.

Um humm, I had a starting point, which was probably the late ‘30’s and I moved on after that into the early to middle ‘40’s and then I really began getting interested in the early ‘30’s and the ‘20’s. And so I was moving in all sorts of directions. I know there are a lot on youngsters today, they’ll start with maybe Elvin Jones or Tony Williams, which for them is going back 30 or 35 years. And that’s like the beginning of the history of jazz drumming, but you just have to work back further and further. So I started with what I really enjoyed very much, which was Gene Krupa. And like I said, Joe Morello and Louie Bellson and Buddy Rich, and Papa Jo Jones, and was going in different directions as far as a yearly category, you know, it was mentioned. So that’s what I did. I tried to

embrace, ultimately, as many of the great, great drummers, far back toward the beginning of this century and on up to somebody I might meet tomorrow afternoon or somebody that I heard play last week. And I love them all.
